name: Cueits
tagline: A small paid web utility in the cue, prompt and reminder corner of productivity; exact feature set not independently verified at draft time.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Public information on this one is thin, so treat the confidence rating as the headline. What is clear from the shape of the product is that it sits in the cue and reminder category, which is the most cloneable genre in all of software: a list, a schedule, and something that pokes you at the right moment. An agent can produce a local version of that core loop in a session, and it will feel fine on a laptop. The gaps are the usual ones and they are not small: real mobile push, background delivery when your machine is asleep, and sync across devices are all infrastructure problems rather than UI problems. If the paid product's actual value turns out to be a specific integration or a mobile app, the DIY build is a toy next to it.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you write cues, attach a schedule or trigger, and get nudged with a browser notification plus a daily digest view.
requirements: A browser left open for notifications to fire, or a machine that stays awake
Optional: an SMTP account in .env if you want email nudges instead of browser ones
whatYouLose: Reliable mobile push, the one thing a reminder tool actually lives or dies on
Delivery when your laptop is closed, unless you park the build on a small always-on box
Cross device sync, so your phone and desktop cues drift apart
Whatever integrations the paid product ships with, which is the part you cannot guess at from the outside
Someone else worrying about timezone and daylight saving edge cases, which will bite you
moatNotes: Reminder products compete on whether the nudge arrives at all, on the right device, at the right second. That is a delivery problem, not a features problem.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a reminder you did not receive is worse than no reminder, and self-hosted nudges fail quietly. Paying a few dollars a month buys a service that runs when your laptop is shut, pushes to a phone you actually carry, and has already been debugged against timezones, retries and dead notification permissions. The build below covers the thinking part of the loop; the boring reliability part is exactly what the money is for.
notes: Low confidence entry: the category is trivially cloneable, the specific product is not well documented publicly, so the verdict leans on the genre rather than the app.
prompt:
Build a local-first cue and reminder app called Cuebox. Empty folder, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript
- Tailwind CSS for styling, no component library
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/cuebox.db, schema created on first run
- node-cron inside a single server-side scheduler module, started once on boot

Data model:
- cue: id, title, body (markdown, optional), kind ('once' | 'recurring'), dueAt (ISO, for once), cronExpr (for recurring), timezone, active, createdAt
- delivery: id, cueId, firedAt, acknowledgedAt (nullable), snoozedUntil (nullable)

Features in scope:
1. A single-page inbox listing cues grouped into Overdue, Today, Upcoming, Paused.
2. Create and edit cues in a side panel. For recurring cues accept a cron expression and show a plain-English preview plus the next three fire times.
3. Scheduler ticks every 30 seconds, finds due cues, writes a delivery row, and pushes it to the open browser tab over a Server-Sent Events endpoint.
4. Browser Notification API on the client for each incoming delivery. Ask permission once, fall back to an in-page toast if denied.
5. Snooze buttons: 10 minutes, 1 hour, tomorrow 9am. Acknowledge marks the delivery done and, for 'once' cues, deactivates the cue.
6. Optional email fallback: if SMTP_URL and CUE_EMAIL_TO exist in .env, also send a plain-text email per delivery using nodemailer. Skip silently if unset.
7. Keyboard driven: 'n' new cue, 'j'/'k' move selection, 'e' edit, 'x' acknowledge, '/' filter by text.
8. GET /api/export returns all cues and deliveries as JSON. POST /api/import accepts the same shape.

Explicitly out of scope: mobile push, native apps, multi-user auth, sharing, calendar sync, AI anything.

All config in .env, with a .env.example committed. Write a README that states plainly that notifications only fire while the app process is running, and suggests running it on an always-on machine if that matters. Seed the database with three example cues on first run.
